sentences.text: The type specimen, cataloged as UNDG R-1000, preserves a nearly complete skull, a full hindlimb, and several vertebrae.
This single known individual is estimated to have exceeded four meters in total length.
Features such as an incompletely ossified sagittal crest and undeveloped palatine wings suggest the animal may have been a subadult when it died.
Its lower jaw possessed a short symphysis containing only six pairs of functional tooth sockets.
A heavily swollen and ornamented sagittal crest formed a distinct parietal knob on the top of the skull.
Acostasaurus possessed a very large scleral ring, a structure indicating adaptation for vision in deep or murky waters.
Researchers noted that the base of the functional tooth sockets merges with Meckel's canal, a trait similar to that seen in Simolestes.
The genus Acostasaurus was formally described by Gómez Pérez and Noè in 2017.
The large scleral ring indicates that Acostasaurus was adapted to see in deep or turbid waters.
Acostasaurus is classified within the family Pliosauridae.
It belongs to the suborder Pliosauroidea.
This species is distinguished from typical brachauchenine pliosaurs by its caniniform dentition rather than longirostrine homodont dentition.
Although researchers compared Acostasaurus to various brachauchenine taxa, they found that referring it to that subfamily remains problematic.
Fossils of Acostasaurus date to the Barremian stage.
These fossils have been found in the Barremian-aged Paja Formation in Colombia.
Acostasaurus lived between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago during the Barremian.
